editorial.titleTr: Defense Minister Nominee Faces Mockery: Will He Command 500,000 Troops?
summaryTr: Defense Minister nominee Kang Shin-chul mocked over real estate suspicions at confirmation hearing.
Explanations lack persuasiveness on eldest son's asset acquisition and reporting omissions.
Concerns over defense capability gap if moral controversy persists.
editorial.bodyTr: Defense Minister nominee Kang Shin-chul faced ridicule at his confirmation hearing over allegations that he improperly acquired an apartment through a special supply program for residents displaced by redevelopment. The nominee claimed he was unaware of his eldest son's purchase of real estate worth around 700 million won and his failure to report assets, but his explanation lacked persuasiveness. The article pointed out that if the ethical controversy remains unresolved, it could hamper efforts to restore military morale and impede progress on major security issues.

editorials.titleTr: Mifepristone Introduction Requires Strict Controls to Prevent Misuse
summaryTr: Government Officially Adopts Mifepristone Within Legal Framework Seven Years After Abortion Ban Ruled Unconstitutional
Targeting First-Quarter Distribution Next Year, Review Proceeding With Condition of Use Within 9 Weeks of Pregnancy
Two-Year Period of Management Through Doctor Prescriptions at Medical Institutions to Fill Legal Void
editorials.bodyTr: The government has formally announced the introduction of mifepristone, an abortion medication, into the official medical system seven years after the Constitutional Court ruled the abortion ban incompatible with the constitution. The government is targeting distribution in the first quarter of next year and has conducted reviews under the condition of use within nine weeks of pregnancy. The government has instructed healthcare institutions to prepare a management system in which doctors directly prescribe the medication over a two-year period to fill the legal vacuum.

editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Prosecution Withdrawal and Reelection Debate Must End for Press Conference to Prove Change
summaryTr: President Lee Jae-myung holds a press conference on the 18th, but concrete changes are essential to recover his approval ratings.
He must first end controversies over the dismissal of charges and constitutional revision for consecutive terms, and offer a clear apology for failures in real estate policy.
Without fundamental improvements in inappropriate personnel appointments and the president-centric governing style, the press conference will be meaningless.
editorial.bodyTr:
President Lee Jae-myung has decided to hold a press conference on the 18th amid declining approval ratings for his administration. While he says he will answer questions about pending national issues without restrictions, simply opening a channel for communication will not be enough to win back public trust. An opinion poll released yesterday by the Korean Social Opinion Research Institute showed that negative assessments outweighed positive ones across all age groups, including those in their 40s and 50s who had strongly supported the ruling party. The situation calls for clear reflection on the overall direction of state affairs, which has lost public confidence.

The first matters to address are the withdrawal of prosecution and the proposed constitutional amendment for consecutive reelection, both related to the president's legal risks. The confusion surrounding the withdrawal of prosecution and public skepticism about pursuing a constitutional amendment for reelection have been cited as burdens on state affairs by both the opposition and within the ruling party itself. Since these issues directly concern the president personally, he must end the controversy by explicitly stating that he will abandon efforts to withdraw the prosecution and that under no circumstances will he seek reelection. Abandoning the stubbornness and self-righteousness that shake judicial and constitutional order is the bare minimum starting point for a recovery in approval ratings.

The president must also apologize for the failure of real estate policy that has failed to address citizens' actual living conditions and present supplementary measures. The government has caused market distortions such as soaring jeonse and monthly rental prices through measures like tax pressure on non-resident single-home owners, yet has only cited the justification of eliminating speculation. If the administration fails to demonstrate how it will correct this apparent incompetence and policy misjudgment, it will not be able to suppress the backlash from young people and the middle class that is now emerging.

Decisive action on personnel failures is also necessary. If the government pushes forward with appointments despite putting forward underqualified ministerial candidates and drawing public outrage, the press conference will lose all credibility. In particular, bold measures are needed to make Justice Minister nominee Kim Seung-won, who has caused controversy through inappropriate solicitation, step down voluntarily or withdraw his nomination. Attempting to push through his appointment based on a "toothless confirmation hearing" would only add fuel to public alienation.

President Lee has thus far demonstrated a hands-on governance style in which he directly oversees all matters. As a result, the president's position has become the guideline, rigorous verification has disappeared, and policies disconnected from the people's lives have driven livelihoods into ruin. The public is currently sending a strong signal that it wants sincere apologies about the flawed direction of state affairs and concrete change. If the president says something different, the press conference might as well not happen.

editorial.title: A test of loyalty
editorial.body: Ruling-party backlash over nominee raises questions about investigative independence President Lee Jae Myung recently ordered additional vetting of Kim Ji-yong, whom he nominated to head the Serious Crimes Investigation Agency, which is scheduled to launch early next month. It is necessary to clarify whether there were any problems with the initial vetting, though it had already been completed; above all, the circumstances raise suspicions that Lee's order may have been influenced by strong backlash from hard-liners in the ruling party. Democratic Party of Korea lawmakers Park Ju-min and Kim Yong-min, among others, called for the nomination to be withdrawn. Gyeonggi Gov. Choo Mi-ae, a former Democratic Party lawmaker who chaired the Legislation and Judiciary Committee, criticized the nomination on Sept. 12, saying, “If someone who was in the same boat as Han Dong-hoon becomes the founding head of the Serious Crimes Investigation Agency, is that democratization?” Han, an independent lawmaker, previously served as a prosecutor, justice minister and leader of the opposition People Power Party. Park, Kim and Choo are taking issue with the nominee’s record: While serving at the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office, he opposed the Democratic Party’s push to abolish prosecutors’ supplementary investigative authority. Kim Ji-yong had also joined a statement opposing then-Justice Minister Choo Mi-ae’s request for disciplinary action against then-Prosecutor General Yoon Seok Yeol. If additional vetting uncovers any new serious grounds for disqualification, there would be no need to hesitate to withdraw the nomination. But there would be a problem if the order for additional vetting was issued simply because of backlash from some ruling-party hard-liners. There is a concern that the additional vetting could degenerate into a process for testing the nominee’s political loyalty. The head of the Serious Crimes Investigation Agency is not a position to be filled solely by the standards of reform sought by a particular political faction. How faithfully the nominee has followed their approach to prosecution reform cannot be the key criterion for qualification as head of the agency. The most important qualification for the head of the agency is investigative expertise. For such expertise to be properly exercised, above all, political neutrality and independence must be upheld. The head of the agency should be able to handle even cases that may be politically inconvenient for those in power according to principle and deal with them based on the law and evidence, regardless of whether they involve the ruling or opposition parties.
